text: Given an array of integers called nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. Exactly one solution exists, and you can't use the same element twice.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I return the two indices, not the values; there's exactly one answer, so I don't handle no-solution or ties; and the array isn't sorted?
Correct on all three. Values and target can be negative. Follow-up: can you beat quadratic time?
Let me run through the example. Two, seven, eleven, fifteen, with target nine, gives zero and one, since two plus seven is nine.

Let me think. Brute force checks every pair, which is quadratic. The key reframe: instead of asking which two numbers pair up, I stand at each number and ask what's the one number I need. That's the complement, target minus the current number, and it's uniquely determined. This problem reminds me of the complement lookup pattern with a hash map: the question becomes have I seen that value before, and at which index — and a hash map answers that in constant time.

Value to index. I look up by value — the complement — so the value is the key; and I need to return the index, so the index is the stored data. Storing it the other way around would be useless — I'd have the complement's value but couldn't look it up.

Here's the plan. One: start with an empty map from value to index. Two: for each index, compute the complement, and if it's already in the map, return its index and mine. Three: otherwise, store my own value and index. One thing worth flagging — check the complement before storing myself. If I stored first, an element equal to half the target, like three with target six, would find itself and I'd return i and i, using one element twice. Checking first means the map only holds earlier elements. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Here's the code. One loop: compute the complement, look it up, and if it's there, return both indices; if not, store the current value with its index. The line that's easy to get wrong is the store — it has to come after the lookup, not before, or a number that's half the target pairs with itself. The final return of minus one, minus one is unreachable, since a solution is guaranteed. That's amortized linear time and linear space — one pass, one lookup and one insert per element.
What if the array has duplicate values, like three, three with target six?

It works without any special case. The first three finds an empty map, so it just stores three at index zero. The second three's complement is three, and that's in the map, mapped to index zero — the first three, not the current one. So it returns zero and one. Because I check before storing, the map only ever holds earlier elements, so a duplicate always pairs with the other occurrence, never itself.

Let's dry-run three, two, four with target six — expected one and two. The first two numbers miss, so the map holds three at zero and two at one. The row that matters is the four: its complement is two, which is in the map at index one, so I return one and two — two plus four is six. That matches. Also checked: the first example gives zero and one, and three, three with target six gives zero and one. I verified on three thousand random arrays that it always returns two distinct valid indices summing to target — zero failures.

Time is amortized linear, space is linear — which answers the follow-up: strictly better than quadratic. Oh, one more thing — if the array were sorted and I only needed the values, I'd use two pointers for constant space instead; that's Two Sum Two. And this complement-plus-hash idea is the atom underneath a whole family: Three Sum is fix one number, Two Sum the rest, and Subarray Sum Equals K is the same trick with prefix sums instead of values — have I seen prefix minus K before. So this first problem is really a template.

Excellent. You reframed pairing into a complement lookup, got the check-before-store ordering and why it prevents self-pairing, and connected it to Three Sum and prefix-sum problems. Clean pass on the classic.
